1840s-priest.title: A priest in daguerreotype
1840s-priest.note: The exposure took tens of seconds. He had to quiet his breath and fix his gaze on a point that did not exist. Portraits of that era carry a trace of held breath. No battle, no treaty — just a man deciding to spend money to keep himself. History's thickest layer has always been made of moments like this, with no names.

1843-daguerreotype.title: A man photographed himself into the studio
1843-daguerreotype.note: In 1839 Daguerre announced the daguerreotype. Within a few years someone had turned the lens on himself. Before that, leaving a likeness of “I am here” took a brush and someone else's hand; after, light could do it alone. What Frame & Grain collects begins at this moment — including this slightly nervous self-portrait.

1852-bridge.title: The bridge at Paralda
1852-bridge.note: A salt print from a waxed-paper negative, of a bridge no one remembers. The photographer had to coat, expose and develop on site, and came away with only a few plates, so every shutter release began with a question: is it worth it? He thought it was. The street corner you photograph today may be looked at this carefully in a hundred years.

1860-taku.title: The Taku Forts: the corner the French stormed
1860-taku.note: An albumen print, 1860. The catalog title says it plainly: “the angle of the Taku Forts through which the French forces entered” — even the direction of the view becomes testimony. These images from the Second Opium War are among the earliest photographic records of China; most of the negatives ended up abroad, and have to be brought back one by one.

1860s-tintype.title: Andy Wilson's tintype
1860s-tintype.note: Tintypes were cheap, fast and hardy — the portrait ordinary people could afford. The catalog calls him a “contraband,” a servant in the Civil War's vocabulary. The name survives; a life is reduced to this small sheet of iron. This is the kind of image Frame & Grain most wants to keep: someone written down in passing by the great sweep of history.

1863-soldier.title: The soldier lying down
1863-soldier.note: A portrait from the American Civil War, and the man is lying down. No charge, no flag, only a pose. Great events are never made only of generals and dates; in the end they land on one specific person — here, not even his name survives.

1871-paris-barricade.title: The barricade on Rue de Castiglione
1871-paris-barricade.note: Paris Commune, 1871, Rue de Castiglione, a barricade built of paving stones. No charge in the photograph, only stacked stone and a few men standing. The longest stretch of an uprising is waiting. The street name survives; the men who stacked the stones do not.

1875-market.title: Market day outside the city wall
1875-market.note: Outside the city wall, stalls set out, someone choosing goods, someone just standing and talking. Nothing happened that day, and precisely for that it was painted. Only with such scenes on the same axis as wars and moon landings does the human world become whole: most days have no title.

1888-eiffel-construction.title: When the tower was half built
1888-eiffel-construction.note: In 1888 Louis-Émile Durandelle photographed the Eiffel Tower under construction. The steel was still a skeleton assembled floor by floor; Paris went about its life at its feet. Later it became the city's signature, but here it looks more like an unfinished building site.

1900-mailcar.title: Boston's mail streetcar
1900-mailcar.note: Ca. 1900, a streetcar in Boston that sorted mail on board. Letters were postmarked and sorted into slots as the car ran along the tracks — how a city actually works is often more honest than any manifesto. We keep it because the earliest shape of “modern life” usually hides in infrastructure like this.

1900-women.title: Two women who left no names
1900-women.note: A cabinet card, ca. 1900. Two women dressed carefully and seated side by side, clearly prepared for the day. The catalog title says only “two unidentified women.” “Unidentified” is not a defect; it is how most people remain in history: seen, not remembered.

1908-boy.title: The boy at the loom
1908-boy.note: A cotton mill in Indiana, around 1908. He stands at the loom, just tall enough to reach the machine. The four characters “Industrial Revolution” land on one person at exactly this height. Frame & Grain puts this on the same timeline as the Moon landing not to elevate it, but to keep the scale from flipping.

1915-suffrage.title: A women's suffrage postcard
1915-suffrage.note: 1915: a postcard meant to be sent, pinned to a desk corner, pushed into a drawer. The movement did not happen only in parliament; it seeped into daily life through paper like this, a penny a sheet. Great events have their own popular circulation history, and it rarely looks like a monument.

1918-influenza-ward.title: 1918: an influenza ward
1918-influenza-ward.note: New Orleans naval hospital, 1918. An influenza patient being treated. The pandemic was later reduced to a number in the millions, but the lens leaves only a bed, a person leaning over, and a curtain someone hung. History's heaviest part often hides in rooms like this, with no sound.

1918-redcross-station.title: A demonstration at a Red Cross first-aid station
1918-redcross-station.note: 1918, at a Red Cross first-aid station, a group demonstrates ambulance work. No patients, no chaos, only neat ranks and carefully laid-out equipment — what the pandemic rehearsed most was “being ready.”

1945-vmail.title: A V-Mail letter
1945-vmail.note: 13 February 1945. To save shipping space, letters home were microfilmed, flown across the ocean, and enlarged again on arrival. Half of war is the front; the other half is the people waiting for a reply. This thin sheet touches both. We collect the letter, not the battle.

1968-earthrise-first.title: Seeing Earthrise for the first time
1968-earthrise-first.note: December 1968. Apollo 8 swung behind the Moon and came back around; Earth suddenly rose above the lunar horizon. Archive number AS08-13-2329. Humans had photographed Earth countless times, but never as “the place we live” rising as a celestial body. Nearly every later claim about the whole begins with this frame.

1969-plaque.title: The plaque left on the Moon
1969-plaque.note: 20 July 1969. A metal plaque was left on the lunar surface: “We came in peace for all mankind.” For the first time, humans placed a sentence addressed to everyone outside the Earth. The date is precise to the day; the subject is “we” — the standard shape of a great event.

1969-saturn.title: Saturn V
1969-saturn.note: The rocket that put people on the Moon. Historical events often need an object to testify: a document, an artefact, a photograph. This frame has no human face, only a machine that was built — perhaps the most honest self-portrait of its era.

1981-sts1.title: STS-1 lifts off
1981-sts1.note: NASA's original caption begins, “After six years of silence.” On 12 April 1981 the shuttle left the launch pad for the first time. Even the official archive could not resist an emotional opening — a measure of how long the wait had been.

2012-earth.title: Looking down from the International Space Station
2012-earth.note: 2012, a frame looking down from low Earth orbit. No borders, no place names, only cloud and sea. The contemporary image that most resembles “a common human history” usually comes from the farthest place from humans — far enough that no one is visible, and yet it is all about people.

2022-artemis.title: Artemis I flight readiness review
2022-artemis.note: August 2022, a flight readiness review in session. History does not happen only at ignition; it forms slowly in countless meeting-room photographs: someone bent over papers, someone facing a screen. We collect these “not yet” images too.

2026-earthset.title: Earthset from Orion
2026-earthset.note: April 2026. As the Orion spacecraft skimmed past the lunar limb, Earth was setting. NASA's caption notes that it echoes the famous “Earthrise.” More than half a century later, the equipment has changed, a generation has changed, and the direction of the gaze has not.

aivazovsky-ninth-wave-1850.title: The Ninth Wave
aivazovsky-ninth-wave-1850.note:
The Ninth Wave shows dawn after a storm. The sea is still torn by huge waves; six survivors cling to a piece of wreckage on the crest; the sky moves from deep blue to orange-gold as sunlight breaks through cloud. The central wave rises like a transparent wall, almost swallowing the figures.

Aivazovsky had not witnessed this particular storm, yet he paints the transparency, foam and refraction of water with extraordinary conviction. He produced thousands of seascapes; this is the most quoted: nature's power and human smallness in one breath.
aivazovsky-ninth-wave-1850.creator: Ivan Aivazovsky

artemisia-judith-1620.title: Judith Slaying Holofernes
artemisia-judith-1620.note:
Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith Beheading Holofernes is more physical and more intimate than Caravaggio's treatment. Judith stands at the bed, sleeves pushed to the elbow, both arms bearing down on the general's shoulder and hair; the maid Abra presses his body from above, the two women completing a task that must be completed. Blood runs down the sheet and stains Judith's cuff.

The painter herself was forced to describe a rape during a 1611 trial, and the picture is often read as revenge. Whether or not that reading is pressed too far, the composition of two women exerting force together is extremely rare in seventeenth-century painting.
artemisia-judith-1620.creator: Artemisia Gentileschi

boecklin-isle-of-the-dead-1883.title: Isle of the Dead
boecklin-isle-of-the-dead-1883.note:
Isle of the Dead shows a cemetery floating on the sea: a rocky island covered with dark cypresses, cliffs rising vertically; a small boat approaches the landing, a figure in white standing aboard, a coffin at the bow. The sky is a heavy grey-blue, the water almost still.

Böcklin does not paint a specific Mediterranean island; he turns death into a space — an island that can be neither reached nor left. It was copied and adapted endlessly, and shaped twentieth-century images of dream and film.
boecklin-isle-of-the-dead-1883.creator: Arnold Böcklin

bosch-garden-earthly-delights-1500.title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
bosch-garden-earthly-delights-1500.note:
The Garden of Earthly Delights is a triptych. The left panel is Eden, where God presents Eve to Adam; the centre is a garden crowded with thousands of naked figures sporting among fruit, pools, birds and beasts; the right is a dark hell where musical instruments become instruments of torture and monsters devour bodies. Closed, the outer wings show a grey creation, the world enclosed in a transparent sphere.

Bosch packs medieval moral allegory, alchemical signs and folk proverb into one visual machine, so that pleasure and punishment follow nose to tail. Whether it is warning, satire or the projection of something repressed has never been settled; that very resistance to decoding is why it still holds viewers five centuries later.
bosch-garden-earthly-delights-1500.creator: Hieronymus Bosch

botticelli-birth-of-venus-1485.title: The Birth of Venus
botticelli-birth-of-venus-1485.note:
Venus rises from the sea on a vast shell, blown ashore by Zephyr and a breeze goddess, while one of the Horae waits with an embroidered mantle. Botticelli abandons the medieval gold ground and lets sea and shore dissolve into pale blue and green; the goddess's weight sits to the right, her hair and drapery blown into continuous curves. Anatomy is not obeyed: the body is stretched and tilted, its outline as crisp as a carved relief.

This "incorrect elegance" is the ideal beauty of the early Renaissance, proportion derived from poetry rather than measurement. The panel belonged to the Medici collection, carried pagan myth into Florentine rooms, and remains one of the most reproduced images of beauty in Western art.
botticelli-birth-of-venus-1485.creator: Sandro Botticelli

botticelli-primavera-1480.title: Primavera
botticelli-primavera-1480.note:
Primavera unfolds like a half-open theatre. On the right, Zephyr pursues a nymph and Flora scatters flowers across the panel; at the centre Venus raises a hand in blessing while blindfolded Cupid aims above her; on the left the Three Graces dance in a ring, with Mercury, his back to us, at the far edge. Orange trees close the dark background, and the grass is studded with hundreds of identifiable flowers.

Botticelli braids pagan myth, spring allegory and Medici court taste into a single horizontal narrative. There is no central focus, yet gaze, gesture and the rhythm of drapery hold the composition together. With The Birth of Venus, it forms the Renaissance's most complete and elegant translation of ancient myth.
botticelli-primavera-1480.creator: Sandro Botticelli

bruegel-hunters-in-snow-1565.title: Hunters in the Snow (Winter)
bruegel-hunters-in-snow-1565.note:
Hunters in the Snow is the coldest and quietest panel of Bruegel's series of the months. Hunters and dogs descend a ridge from the right, their tracks dragging a diagonal line through the snow; village roofs sag under snow on the left, skaters circle a pond beyond, and grey-blue mountains close the horizon. There is no central figure, yet the eye is led along ridge, treeline and ice into the distance.

Bruegel paints northern winter air as something breathable: leaden sky, black trees, dirty snow. The human figures are only part of the landscape, and this "small people, large nature" view echoes later through Dutch landscape painting and Romanticism.
bruegel-hunters-in-snow-1565.creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder

bruegel-tower-of-babel-1563.title: The Tower of Babel
bruegel-tower-of-babel-1563.note:
Bruegel paints the biblical Tower of Babel as a building site: the tower spirals upward, its tiers of arcades, stairs and scaffolding swarming like an anthill; the top has not closed, and red brick alternates with grey stone. At the lower left, King Nimrod rides in with his retinue while workmen still haul blocks.

Bruegel fills this monument to human hubris with Flemish everyday detail, and lets it shadow the commercial fever and fear of linguistic division in sixteenth-century Antwerp. The tower is cut open like a section through history: magnificent, and doomed.
bruegel-tower-of-babel-1563.creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder

caravaggio-calling-of-matthew-1600.title: The Calling of Saint Matthew
caravaggio-calling-of-matthew-1600.note:
The Calling of Saint Matthew takes place in a dim Roman tax collector's room. Christ enters from the right and raises a hand; a shaft of light follows the gesture, crossing the table and landing on Matthew. Seated behind the table, Matthew points at himself as if asking, "Who, me?" A young man beside him counts coins, two others continue talking. Table, stool, money bag and quill are painted as ordinary objects.

Caravaggio places the sacred moment in the most worldly of rooms and lets light, rather than composition, perform the calling. The beam illuminates Matthew and draws a line at the table from which there is no turning back.
caravaggio-calling-of-matthew-1600.creator: Caravaggio

caravaggio-judith-1599.title: Judith Beheading Holofernes
caravaggio-judith-1599.note:
Caravaggio turns the biblical assassination into a murder at the bedside. Judith stands on the right, one hand gripping Holofernes' hair, the other holding the sword; her face recoils, brows knitted, disgust and fear together. The general's body twists on the bed, mouth open, blood jetting from the neck onto white sheets. The maid Abra waits at the left, bag in hand, tense.

Caravaggio refuses to beautify the heroic act: Judith is not an allegory but a woman exerting force and feeling afraid. Extreme chiaroscuro presses the background into black, leaving only skin, linen and blood in the light.
caravaggio-judith-1599.creator: Caravaggio

castiglione-hundred-horses-1728.title: One Hundred Horses
castiglione-hundred-horses-1728.note:
One Hundred Horses is a handscroll painted at the Qing court by the Italian Jesuit Giuseppe Castiglione. More than a hundred horses are dispersed across grassy slopes, streams and trees: standing, rolling, drinking, led by herdsmen. Their bodies are modelled with fine light and shade, while trees, rocks and ground retain Chinese texture strokes and reserved space.

Castiglione brought European perspective, anatomy and chiaroscuro into court painting, and was obliged to compromise with Chinese materials and viewing habits. The result is a hybrid vision: horses in the round, space flat; realism and ornament in the same scroll.
castiglione-hundred-horses-1728.creator: Giuseppe Castiglione

cezanne-mont-sainte-victoire-1904.title: Mont Sainte-Victoire
cezanne-mont-sainte-victoire-1904.note:
Mont Sainte-Victoire was a motif Cézanne returned to again and again in his late years. The mountain is broken into parallel strokes — ochre, grey-green, pale blue — like masonry and like breathing; trees and fields in the foreground have no clear edges, only blocks of colour advancing and receding. Sky and mountain share one scale of tones; space is built not by perspective but by temperature of colour and direction of stroke.

Cézanne painted the same view dozens of times, not to record landscape but to find structure. He moved painting from "what is seen" to "how seeing is organised," a step that Cubism would take up.
cezanne-mont-sainte-victoire-1904.creator: Paul Cézanne

chardin-the-ray-1728.title: The Ray (La Raie)
chardin-the-ray-1728.creator: Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin
chardin-the-ray-1728.note:
Chardin's *The Ray* was his reception piece for the Royal Academy in 1728, and a manifesto for still life. A gutted ray hangs from a hook, its silver belly opened, red entrails spilling; a cat steps among oyster shells on the left, while bottles, a jar, a knife and a white cloth occupy the right. Everything sits on a rough stone ledge. There is no myth and no allegory, only the smell of a kitchen.

Chardin uses thick white highlights for the wet skin of the fish and a dark brown ground to push the objects forward. He makes the everyday worth looking at, preparing the way for Courbet and Manet's respect for ordinary things.

commons-1900-beijing.title: Beijing in 1900
commons-1900-beijing.note: Beijing in 1900: city walls, street corners and passers-by all caught on the same negative. China was being photographed earlier than people usually assume; most of these images are scattered in collections abroad, like finding your own old letters in someone else's drawer. Frame & Grain wants to bring them back, one by one.

commons-1912-titanic.title: Titanic leaving Southampton
commons-1912-titanic.note: 10 April 1912, departure. No iceberg, no band, just a ship leaving the dock as if nothing were about to happen. The story told for a century is all compressed into this departure photograph where nothing happens — the most understated foreshadowing an image can offer.

commons-1930-shanghai.title: Nanjing Road in the 1930s
commons-1930-shanghai.note: Signs, trams, pedestrians: a street that writes its own decade plainly enough to need no date. The word “era” always lands on one specific street — who walks there, what the shops sell, what typeface the signs use. This unsigned street view is closer to its time than many chronicles.

commons-1936-migrant.title: Migrant Mother
commons-1936-migrant.note: March 1936, Dorothea Lange pressed the shutter at a pea-picking camp in California. The macro numbers of the Depression become one face and several children turning away. Later it became the cover of an entire era — but on the day, no one knew.

commons-1944-dday.title: “Into the Jaws of Death”
commons-1944-dday.note: 6 June 1944, Omaha Beach. The archive number is 23-0455M; the title is “Into the Jaws of Death.” Sometimes a great event leaves only a number, a group of backs facing the camera, and a metaphor even the official record could not resist.

commons-1945-hiroshima.title: Hiroshima, after the bomb
commons-1945-hiroshima.note: An aerial photograph from August 1945. Almost no detail survives, only a city erased flat. Some images should be neither beautified nor omitted. Frame & Grain keeps the record without judging, but keeps its weight — and the few seconds that make you stop.

commons-1945-iwojima.title: The flag on Iwo Jima
commons-1945-iwojima.note: 23 February 1945, Joe Rosenthal. The moment was later printed on stamps, cast in bronze, reproduced without end. How a photograph becomes memory, and how memory then covers the photograph, is itself a history worth archiving.

commons-1969-aldrin.title: The photographer reflected in the visor
commons-1969-aldrin.note: 20 July 1969. Aldrin stands on the Moon; in his gold visor, Armstrong is reflected holding the camera. Humanity's farthest journey still comes down to two people: one photographed, one photographing. Every grand narrative breaks down into this division of labour.

commons-1969-bootprint.title: One footprint
commons-1969-bootprint.note: To test whether the lunar soil would hold, Aldrin pressed down a boot print and took a photograph. No wind, no rain; it will probably stay for a long time. The quietest evidence left by something as large as the Moon landing is this — great and small events belong on the same axis.

commons-1989-berlin.title: Juggling on the Berlin Wall
commons-1989-berlin.note: November 1989. The Wall had not fallen yet, and someone was already up on it, juggling. The most moving evidence of a turning point is often not the official photograph but someone's improvisation: a structure built to divide suddenly became a stage.

constable-hay-wain-1821.title: The Hay Wain
constable-hay-wain-1821.note:
The Hay Wain shows a shallow river, a hay wagon crossing it, and a farmhouse. Trees cast shadow on the left; on the right the sky suddenly opens, clouds blown apart; the wagon stands midstream, horses drinking, Suffolk fields beyond.

Constable insisted on painting outdoors, treating English weather as a changing condition rather than a backdrop. The farmhouse is Willy Lott's cottage, a place he had known since childhood. This stubborn attachment to local ground gave landscape painting everyday weight for the first time.
constable-hay-wain-1821.creator: John Constable

courbet-painters-studio-1855.title: The Painter's Studio
courbet-painters-studio-1855.note:
The Painter's Studio carries the subtitle "A real allegory summing up seven years of my artistic and moral life." At the centre, Courbet sits at his easel painting a landscape, a nude model and a boy beside him. On the right are his friends and supporters — Baudelaire, Proudhon, Champfleury and others; on the left, ordinary people from daily life: workers, peasants, beggars, a widow.

Courbet moves "society" into the studio and puts artistic production and political stance in the same room. It is both a challenge to the Academy and a Realist manifesto: the painter does not paint myth, but the people he sees.
courbet-painters-studio-1855.creator: Gustave Courbet

david-death-of-marat-1793.title: The Death of Marat
david-death-of-marat-1793.note:
The Death of Marat turns an assassinated politician into a martyr. Marat lies dead in his bath, body sliding along the diagonal, quill still in his right hand, a petition with a supplicant's name in his left; on the wooden block sit inkwell, papers and a knife. The background is a blank dark field, with no street and no assassin.

David omits the blood and chaos of the scene, leaving only a quiet body that reads almost like an icon. It is the model of revolutionary propaganda: it does not report facts, it manufactures an image worth believing in.
david-death-of-marat-1793.creator: Jacques-Louis David
david-death-of-marat-1793.holding: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium

david-oath-of-horatii-1784.title: Oath of the Horatii
david-oath-of-horatii-1784.note:
Oath of the Horatii turns a moment of Roman history into theatre. Three brothers stand shoulder to shoulder before their father, arms extended towards the swords; the father raises the three blades, an archway and shadow behind him. On the right, the women collapse together, mother and sisters bowing their heads, knowing the war will cost them brothers or husbands.

David uses vertical columns, hard contours and a nearly brushless surface to turn Neoclassical "virtue" into geometry. Male bodies are straight lines, female bodies curves; oath and grief are divided between the two sides of the canvas.
david-oath-of-horatii-1784.creator: Jacques-Louis David

degas-dance-class-1874.title: The Dance Class
degas-dance-class-1874.note:
The Dance Class shows a rehearsal room of the Paris Opéra ballet. At the centre an elderly ballet master leans on a long staff, addressing a group of girls in white tutus; some listen, others scratch their backs, adjust a shoulder strap or drift off. A diagonal cuts the room, and mirror, piano and floor push the space back.

Degas does not seek stage perfection but the fatigue, waiting and small gestures of rehearsal. Trained in Ingresque drawing, he uses pastel-like colour and asymmetric composition to make the backstage the proper subject of modern painting.
degas-dance-class-1874.creator: Edgar Degas

delacroix-liberty-1830.title: Liberty Leading the People
delacroix-liberty-1830.note:
Liberty Leading the People turns the barricades of the July Revolution of 1830 into myth. Liberty stands half-naked at the centre, the tricolour raised in her right hand, a musket in her left, striding over bodies. Around her are a bourgeois in a top hat, a youth with pistols, a worker kneeling on the ground; Paris rooftops and smoke behind.

Delacroix paints the revolution not as an orderly demonstration but as a chaotic, bloody advance. The tricolour is the brightest colour in the picture, a lighthouse drawing the crowd towards it. The painting later became one of the symbols of the French Republic.
delacroix-liberty-1830.creator: Eugène Delacroix

delaunay-eiffel-tower-1911.title: Eiffel Tower (Tour Eiffel)
delaunay-eiffel-tower-1911.creator: Robert Delaunay
delaunay-eiffel-tower-1911.holding: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
delaunay-eiffel-tower-1911.note:
Delaunay turns the Eiffel Tower into a rotating column of colour. The iron structure is broken into red-brown, orange and grey-blue facets; clouds burst in rings, and the surrounding apartment blocks tilt toward the tower. He does not use the monochrome analysis of Cubism; colour itself creates space — warm planes advance, cool planes recede, and the iron lattice appears and disappears between them.

Paris in 1911 was a city of aeroplanes, posters, the Metro and electric light. The painting turns 'simultaneity' into visual experience: you cannot see the tower all at once, only feel several of its faces at the same time.

duccio-maesta-1308.title: Maestà (Madonna Enthroned with Saints and Angels)
duccio-maesta-1308.creator: Duccio di Buoninsegna
duccio-maesta-1308.holding: Museo dell'Opera Metropolitana del Duomo, Siena
duccio-maesta-1308.medium: Tempera and gold leaf on panel
duccio-maesta-1308.note:
*Maestà* was the front panel of Duccio's double-sided altarpiece for Siena Cathedral, carried through the streets in 1311 like a relic. The Virgin sits on a throne with the Christ Child, surrounded by saints and angels; the gold ground compresses the crowd into a luminous plane. Duccio does not abandon Byzantine majesty — the blue mantle, long fingers and ceremonial symmetry are inherited from the East — but he lets figures turn, whisper and lean, gives drapery real weight at the knee, and opens a shallow space behind the throne.

The result is a sacred image that begins to breathe. It shows that the Renaissance did not appear only in Florence: in Siena, devotional painting had already become a stage for human gesture.

durer-self-portrait-1500.title: Self-Portrait at the Age of 28
durer-self-portrait-1500.note:
In 1500 Dürer painted himself frontally, symmetrically, staring directly at the viewer: long hair and beard falling to either side like a Christ figure, his right hand laid across his chest. The black ground makes face and golden hair luminous, and the fur collar is painted hair by hair. The Latin inscription and his "AD" monogram appear at the right, dated at the threshold of a new century.

Dürer borrows the frontal composition of Christ imagery and raises the artist's self-awareness to something close to sacred. It is read as a manifesto of the Northern Renaissance portrait: the painter is no longer a mere craftsman but a creator sanctioned by God.
durer-self-portrait-1500.creator: Albrecht Dürer

el-greco-view-of-toledo-1600.title: View of Toledo
el-greco-view-of-toledo-1600.note:
El Greco's View of Toledo omits the city's most obvious landmark, the cathedral, and paints instead a city besieged by storm. The alcázar sits on a hill at the left, roofs and spires crowd the middle, and the Tagus bends around the right. Sky occupies most of the canvas, rolling in lead and green, a lightning bolt cracking through it.

This is less a topographic portrait than an inner landscape. El Greco abandons Italianate depth and lets the city float in night; buildings are stretched and twisted, their edges uncertain. Toledo becomes not geography but a symbol of faith and decline together.
el-greco-view-of-toledo-1600.creator: El Greco
el-greco-view-of-toledo-1600.holding: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

fan-kuan-travelers-1025.title: Travelers Among Mountains and Streams
fan-kuan-travelers-1025.note:
Travelers Among Mountains and Streams is the summit of Northern Song landscape. A vast central peak presses forward, its summit lost in mist; a waterfall falls at the right, and at the foot a path carries a train of pack donkeys and two travelers. The figures are almost invisible, placed low in the picture to measure the mountain's height.

Fan Kuan builds the weight of rock from dense "raindrop" texture strokes, layering ink until the mass feels like something that would actually block the road. He seeks not the picturesque but the pressure of a mountain that is simply there.
fan-kuan-travelers-1025.creator: Fan Kuan

fragonard-the-swing-1767.title: The Swing
fragonard-the-swing-1767.note:
The Swing takes Rococo frivolity to its limit. A young woman sits on a swing in the shade, her skirt flying, one shoe kicked into the air; her lover leans out of the bushes at the left to look up, while an older man pulls the ropes at the right rear, apparently unaware. Foliage encloses the scene, and light falls like stage lighting on the pink dress.

Fragonard uses a swirling composition, lifted cloth and a voyeur's gaze to make play the entire content of the picture. It is both a record of eighteenth-century aristocratic amusement and the most famous, most imitable image of Rococo art.
fragonard-the-swing-1767.creator: Jean-Honoré Fragonard

friedrich-wanderer-1818.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
friedrich-wanderer-1818.note:
Wanderer above the Sea of Fog places a man on a rocky summit, his back to us, facing a churning sea of mist. He wears a dark green coat, leans on a cane, hair blown by wind; distant peaks rise through the fog like islands or unknown borders. Below is a deep valley, above a pale sky.

Friedrich uses the Rückenfigur to make the viewer gaze with the figure in the painting. This man is neither hero nor tourist but someone who loses his sense of scale before the infinite. The Romantic sublime is exactly this grandeur mixed with unease.
friedrich-wanderer-1818.creator: Caspar David Friedrich

gauguin-where-do-we-come-from-1898.title: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?
gauguin-where-do-we-come-from-1898.note:
Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going? is Gauguin's largest painting from his Tahiti years. The composition reads from right to left — infant, woman, old person — like a genesis without words. A central figure reaches for fruit, surrounded by blue and green shadow; sea, mountains and a shrine lie behind. The title is inscribed at the lower left like an epitaph on a wall.

Gauguin is not telling a specific story but assembling three questions from bodies, colour and symbol. He turns the colonial "elsewhere" into a philosophical space, and hides his own anxiety inside those still, almost sculptural figures.
gauguin-where-do-we-come-from-1898.creator: Paul Gauguin

giotto-lamentation-1305.title: Lamentation
giotto-lamentation-1305.note:
In the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, Giotto turned the Byzantine icon into bodies that weigh and breathe. Mary bends close to Christ's face, John throws his arms wide, Mary Magdalene holds the feet; a diagonal rock ledge drives the eye down to the dead figure and presses the whole group into the lower left corner. In the sky, angels weep, their grief almost visible.

Giotto set the scene on grey-blue rock and earth rather than against a gold ground, replacing symbolic order with volume, spatial depth and recognisable expression. Drapery acquires thickness, faces acquire shadow, and grief acquires different degrees. Art history often treats this moment as the point where Western painting turns from icon towards nature.
giotto-lamentation-1305.creator: Giotto di Bondone

goya-saturn-1820.title: Saturn Devouring His Son
goya-saturn-1820.note:
Saturn Devouring His Son is the most appalling of Goya's Black Paintings. Saturn appears as a mad old man, eyes staring, mouth wide, both hands gripping a small body whose head and arm have already been bitten away. The background is black; only flesh and white cloth catch the light.

In his late years Goya shut himself in the Quinta del Sordo and painted these works directly onto the walls. They were neither commissions nor exhibition pieces, more like a private record of a man fighting fear. Myth loses its allegory here and leaves only violence itself.
goya-saturn-1820.creator: Francisco Goya
goya-saturn-1820.medium: Oil on plaster transferred to canvas

goya-third-of-may-1814.title: The Third of May 1808
goya-third-of-may-1814.note:
The Third of May 1808 records a night execution of civilians by Napoleon's troops in Madrid. On the left, a rank of soldiers raises muskets, backs to the viewer; on the right, some of the condemned have already fallen, others cover their faces, and at the centre a man in a white shirt throws his arms wide and looks straight into the guns. A lantern behind him turns the darkness into a stage.

Goya paints not the triumph of heroes but fear, blood and bodies that cannot resist. The man in white is lit like a Christ, yet he is not divine, only a person about to die. The picture is often taken as the beginning of the modern image of war: no longer generals, but the killed.
goya-third-of-may-1814.creator: Francisco Goya

gris-portrait-of-picasso-1912.title: Portrait of Pablo Picasso
gris-portrait-of-picasso-1912.creator: Juan Gris
gris-portrait-of-picasso-1912.note:
In 1912 Juan Gris painted the most famous portrait of his circle: Picasso. The face is cut into facets, front, side and top view appearing at once; grey-blue, ochre and cool white are pressed into an almost monochrome chord. Gris does not simply 'break' Picasso; he rebuilds the expression geometrically — eyes as two slopes, the nose a folded line, the hand a sheet of paper.

Diagonals in the background interlock with the triangles of the collar, turning the portrait into architecture. It marks Analytical Cubism moving from dismantling objects to constructing a picture, and Gris becoming more than a follower.

gu-kaizhi-admonitions-scroll-400.title: Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies
gu-kaizhi-admonitions-scroll-400.note:
Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies is among the earliest surviving Chinese handscrolls of figure painting, generally regarded as a Tang-dynasty copy after Gu Kaizhi. It illustrates twelve passages from Zhang Hua's Admonitions in the form of nine surviving scenes: Lady Feng shielding the emperor from a bear, Lady Ban declining the imperial carriage, and court ladies at their toilet or seated in conversation. Draperies lift and flow; lines are fine and unbroken, like silk spun by a silkworm.

There is no perspective and no shadow, yet rhythm of line, distance between figures and blank space organise the narrative. It is both a moral textbook and an image-history of palace women's lives. It entered Britain after the Boxer upheaval in 1900 and is now in the British Museum.
gu-kaizhi-admonitions-scroll-400.creator: Gu Kaizhi (attributed)

hiroshige-sudden-shower-1857.title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
hiroshige-sudden-shower-1857.note:
Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake shows a wooden bridge over the Sumida River as a rainstorm drives pedestrians across it: some open umbrellas, some hunch their shoulders, some simply get wet. Rain is cut as dense diagonal lines; river, roofs and the far bank are flattened into grey-blue silhouettes.

Hiroshige does not paint the storm's centre but the moment rain lands on people. That rhythm of diagonals fascinated Van Gogh, who copied the print in oil, turning the rain into thick strokes of paint.
hiroshige-sudden-shower-1857.creator: Utagawa Hiroshige

hokusai-great-wave-1831.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
hokusai-great-wave-1831.note:
The Great Wave off Kanagawa is the most famous print from Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. An enormous wave dominates the sheet: its crest opens like talons, three transport boats are pushed beneath it, boatmen crouching low; far away Mount Fuji is almost only a triangle, resting quietly at the end of the wave.

Hokusai printed the wave in layers of Prussian blue, from deep indigo to pale white, cutting the sea into translucent blades. He puts the violence of an instant and eternal stillness in one composition: the wave will fall, Fuji will not.
hokusai-great-wave-1831.creator: Katsushika Hokusai

huang-gongwang-fuchun-1350.title: Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains
huang-gongwang-fuchun-1350.note:
Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains was begun when Huang Gongwang was seventy-nine and completed over several years. Pale ink and dry brush describe mountains, villages, pine groves and fishing boats along the Fuchun River; the strokes are loose, like traces of repeated breathing. Mountains do not press, water does not clamour; the whole scroll is an extended walk.

In the early Qing, a collector had the scroll burned to accompany him in death. Rescued, it was split in two: the first section, Remaining Mountain, is in the Zhejiang Provincial Museum; the later section, the Wuyongshi scroll, is in the National Palace Museum, Taipei. Its fate became the most famous "beauty of the fragment" in Chinese painting.
huang-gongwang-fuchun-1350.creator: Huang Gongwang

ingres-grande-odalisque-1814.title: La Grande Odalisque
ingres-grande-odalisque-1814.note:
La Grande Odalisque shows a concubine reclining on a divan. Her back is turned, her head over her shoulder, blue turban and gold fabric enclosing the body; a peacock fan, hookah and drapery fill a closed interior. Her spine is elongated, the right leg gains an extra joint, and the curve of the body defies anatomy.

Ingres does not care about anatomical correctness; he wants continuous line and smooth skin. The painting imagines "the Orient" as a languid, viewable space, and pushes Neoclassical line to the edge of abstraction.
ingres-grande-odalisque-1814.creator: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres

kandinsky-composition-vii-1913.title: Composition VII
kandinsky-composition-vii-1913.note:
Composition VII is the summit of Kandinsky's abstract painting. There are no recognisable objects, only enormous colour masses, arcs, black lines and dense strokes in rotation; the centre reads as an explosion, the edges as fragments being drawn in. Colours push against one another; red, blue, yellow and green argue and reconcile in the same space.

Kandinsky compared painting to music: not describing the world but acting directly on feeling. He made dozens of studies for this picture, and what remains is a visual event in which apocalypse and rebirth happen at once.
kandinsky-composition-vii-1913.creator: Wassily Kandinsky

kirchner-street-berlin-1913.title: Street, Berlin
kirchner-street-berlin-1913.note:
Street, Berlin shows two intersecting city streets. In the foreground two women in fashionable black clothes and exaggerated hats, their faces reduced to sharp, almost mask-like triangles; the street is cut into diagonals, pedestrians bent like paper figures in wind.

Kirchner turns urban stimulus, speed and unease into visual tension: acid pink, green and black, short and sharp strokes. Expressionism does not care whether the street is correct; it cares about the vibration the city produces in the body.
kirchner-street-berlin-1913.creator: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner
kirchner-street-berlin-1913.holding: The Museum of Modern Art, New York

klimt-the-kiss-1908.title: The Kiss
klimt-the-kiss-1908.note:
The Kiss shows two figures kneeling at the edge of a flower meadow: the man bends over the woman, her face tilted up, eyes closed. Their bodies are wrapped in a vast gold cloak covered with circles, rectangles and eye-like shapes; his garment is striped black and white, hers patterned with coloured dots. The background is a shimmering gold field, mosaic and night sky at once.

Klimt pushes Vienna Secession ornament to its limit: love is not a narrative but a state of being enclosed. Gold leaf removes weight from the picture and lifts the couple out of reality into an eternal pattern.
klimt-the-kiss-1908.creator: Gustav Klimt
klimt-the-kiss-1908.medium: Oil on canvas with gold leaf

leonardo-last-supper-1495.title: The Last Supper
leonardo-last-supper-1495.note:
On the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Leonardo stages the Last Supper in a room built by one-point perspective. The twelve apostles are arranged in four groups of three, rippling outward from the centre. Christ has just said, "One of you will betray me"; his hands lie open on the table, while Judas, in shadow, clutches his purse and leans back. The vanishing point sits at Christ's head, and the long table lines gather every voice towards the centre.

Because Leonardo worked in dry tempera and oil rather than true fresco, the painting began to flake soon after completion. What survives is an image endlessly patched by time; its choreography of human psychology remains a primer of Western narrative painting.
leonardo-last-supper-1495.creator: Leonardo da Vinci

leonardo-mona-lisa-1503.title: Mona Lisa
leonardo-mona-lisa-1503.note:
What stays with the viewer is not the smile but the uncertainty: there are no eyebrows, and the corners of the eyes and mouth are blurred past definition; the horizon behind her sits at different heights on either side, roads and water receding into distance. Leonardo's sfumato lets form dissolve into air while pinning the viewer's attention to the face. She is said to be the wife of a Florentine merchant, Lisa Gherardini, though her identity has never been settled.

The painting became a global image after its theft in 1911 and is now the most visited work in the Louvre. Its real revolution is that a portrait ceases to be a record of appearance and becomes a person who seems to think and to look back.
leonardo-mona-lisa-1503.creator: Leonardo da Vinci

lnk-bm.title: The British Museum · Collection images
lnk-bm.note: Open, but explicitly non-commercial. The moment a site runs ads, takes sponsorship or funnels traffic, this material has to come down wholesale. So it sits apart in a text-only link card, governed by the usage-mode switch — no image hidden, no line crossed.

lnk-dpm.title: The Palace Museum · Digital Cultural Relics
lnk-dpm.note: The copyright notice is unambiguous: no commercial use, no systematic extraction, no robotic harvesting, and no building of a similar database. So Frame & Grain keeps only an index card and a link — no image fetched, none cached. The red line is not an obstacle; it is what lets an archive like this last.

lnk-loc.title: Library of Congress · Unassessed images
lnk-loc.note: “No known restrictions” sounds like a pass, but it only means the library found no restrictions. Not finding one is not the same as none existing. Records like this wait in the verification pool until first publication and rights status are checked one by one.

malevich-black-square-1915.title: Black Square
malevich-black-square-1915.note:
Black Square does not depict an object but a gesture: a black quadrilateral on a white ground, its edges not quite straight, the brushwork faintly visible. Malevich hung it in the corner of the 1915 "0.10" exhibition like an icon, so that viewers encountered "nothing" where a holy image would normally stand.

It announced Suprematism: painting no longer imitates nature or tells stories but returns to the elementary form and colour. The black square is not an end but a door — beyond it lie the white, empty canvases.
malevich-black-square-1915.creator: Kazimir Malevich

manet-bar-folies-bergere-1882.title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
manet-bar-folies-bergere-1882.note:
A Bar at the Folies-Bergère shows the last night of a Paris music hall. A barmaid stands behind the counter, both hands resting on the marble, a flower at her breast; glasses, bottles and a plate of oranges are arranged in front of her. The mirror behind her reflects the whole hall: chandeliers, audience, boxes, and a man speaking to her — the place where the viewer actually stands.

Manet paints the reflection not quite correctly and lets the perspective slip. The barmaid's expression is blank, neither welcoming nor refusing. The picture becomes a defining image of modern city life: crowd, light, consumption, and a person who cannot be reached.
manet-bar-folies-bergere-1882.creator: Édouard Manet

manet-dejeuner-sur-herbe-1863.title: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe
manet-dejeuner-sur-herbe-1863.note:
Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe places a nude woman and two fully dressed men on grass outside Paris. The woman sits at the left, knees drawn up, looking straight out of the picture; the men talk, apparently unconcerned. Another woman bends by the stream behind. Light falls through leaves, and the figures seem pasted onto a single plane.

Manet borrows the composition of Giorgione's Pastoral Concert but removes myth and idyll. The nude is no longer a goddess, only a Parisian woman at lunch; this unexplained juxtaposition made the painting one of the first scandals of modern art.
manet-dejeuner-sur-herbe-1863.creator: Édouard Manet

manet-olympia-1863.title: Olympia
manet-olympia-1863.note:
Olympia replaces the Titianesque reclining nude with the reality of nineteenth-century Paris. Olympia lies on a bed in slippers and a black ribbon, looking directly at the viewer; behind her a black maid holds flowers, and a black cat stands at her feet, tail up. Bed, bouquet and shawl are painted flatly and directly, without classical softness.

The painting caused a scandal at the 1865 Salon: the problem was not nudity but her gaze. She is no longer an object to be looked at but someone who looks back. Manet's flat paint and hard black-white contrasts break the viewing contract that had governed the nude since the Renaissance.
manet-olympia-1863.creator: Édouard Manet

masaccio-expulsion-1427.title: The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden
masaccio-expulsion-1427.note:
In the Brancacci Chapel in Florence, Masaccio made shame a matter of bodily weight. Adam and Eve, naked, are driven out from the right; Eve lifts her head and opens her mouth, her hands covering her sex, while Adam bows and hides his face behind his arm, his feet planted in real shadow. There is almost no landscape, only an archway and a strip of ground, yet anatomy, foreshortening and strong chiaroscuro make the scene unusually concrete.

It is often called the first Renaissance image to place the human figure truly at its centre: the angel's sword points outward, but what pierces the viewer is the way the two figures can find nowhere to put their hands and feet. Masaccio died before he was thirty, yet this fresco became a point of return for Leonardo and Michelangelo after him.
masaccio-expulsion-1427.creator: Masaccio

michelangelo-creation-of-adam-1511.title: The Creation of Adam
michelangelo-creation-of-adam-1511.note:
Michelangelo compresses the act of creation into two hands about to touch. Adam lies half-awake on green earth, his body only just kindled; God rushes forward through cloud, his mantle swelling like a sail, angels and wind packed around him. A tiny gap remains between the fingertips, and that gap is what charges the whole ceiling.

With sculptural nudity, violent torsion and almost no setting, Michelangelo turns "man made in God's image" into a tension between flesh and spirit. Adam's gaze is languid and unfocused; God's is urgent and intent. In this instant, creator and created are anything but equal.
michelangelo-creation-of-adam-1511.creator: Michelangelo Buonarroti

millet-the-gleaners-1857.title: The Gleaners
millet-the-gleaners-1857.note:
The Gleaners shows three peasant women bending to pick up scattered grain after the harvest. Their bodies fold almost to the right angle, hands reaching the ground; behind them stand haystacks, harvesters and a pale gold sky. There is no story, only repeated labour and a heavy horizon.

Millet gives the least regarded work of his time a monumental scale: three figures like low sculptures, silent, solid, asking for no pity. Conservative critics read it as a dangerous manifesto when it was shown, because it gave poverty dignity and volume.
millet-the-gleaners-1857.creator: Jean-François Millet

mondrian-composition-red-blue-yellow-193.title: Composition II in Red, Blue and Yellow
mondrian-composition-red-blue-yellow-193.creator: Piet Mondrian
mondrian-composition-red-blue-yellow-193.note:
Mondrian's *Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow* contains only black lines, white ground and three primary planes. A large red rectangle dominates; blue sits at lower left, a small yellow at lower right; the black lines move asymmetrically, thicker here, thinner there, seeking balance rather than executing a grid.

Mondrian called this relationship Neo-Plasticism: horizontal and vertical stand for the two basic forces of the universe, primary colours for pure energy, white for space. There is no story, yet the painting asks for prolonged looking: with every shift of attention, the weight of the colours changes.

monet-impression-sunrise-1872.title: Impression, Sunrise
monet-impression-sunrise-1872.note:
Impression, Sunrise shows dawn in the port of Le Havre. The sun is an orange-red dot; mist divides the water into grey-blue and pale violet; cranes, chimneys and masts blur in the distance, while a small boat cuts the surface in the foreground with a few short strokes.

Monet does not draw outlines; he records light in the air at a particular moment. The critic Louis Leroy borrowed the title to mock these painters as "Impressionists," and the name was taken up by the group. Modern painting acquired its name through a misreading.
monet-impression-sunrise-1872.creator: Claude Monet

moreau-jupiter-semele-1895.title: Jupiter and Semele
moreau-jupiter-semele-1895.note:
Jupiter and Semele shows the moment the mortal Semele asks to see the god in his true form. Jupiter sits on a throne at the centre, a great serpent coiled at his breast, surrounded by tiers of gold ornament and deities; Semele reclines in the foreground, her body already pierced by divine light, almost dissolving.

Moreau paints myth as a palace of symbols: colour like enamel, line like jewellery, no depth, only endless ornament. Symbolism here is not storytelling; the image itself becomes a labyrinth the eye can enter again and again.
moreau-jupiter-semele-1895.creator: Gustave Moreau

morisot-the-cradle-1872.title: The Cradle
morisot-the-cradle-1872.note:
The Cradle shows the painter's sister Edma seated beside a cot, watching her sleeping baby through a gauze curtain. Her left arm supports her head, her right hand rests on the cot's edge; the veil lies over the child's face like mist. Greys, pale blues and pinks dominate, and outlines are almost absent.

Morisot was the most important woman in the Impressionist group, and she painted not the spectacle of public space but the quiet interior of the family. The pose of watching is tender, but also a little tired and absent.
morisot-the-cradle-1872.creator: Berthe Morisot

munch-the-scream-1893.title: The Scream
munch-the-scream-1893.note:
The Scream shows a bridge beside the Oslo fjord. The central figure covers his ears, mouth open, face twisted like a skull; behind him the sky turns in orange-red bands, water is deep blue, and two dark figures walk away. The railing cuts a diagonal out of the picture, as if the viewer were being pushed forward too.

In his diary Munch described hearing "a great, infinite scream from nature." It is not a person screaming so much as an environment pressing on one person. The image became the universal sign of modern anxiety, copied and parodied countless times, and still effective.
munch-the-scream-1893.creator: Edvard Munch

ni-zan-woods-valleys-1355.title: Woods and Valleys of Mount Yu
ni-zan-woods-valleys-1355.note:
Woods and Valleys of Mount Yu is Ni Zan's typical "one river, two banks" composition: a few sparse trees and a rocky slope in the foreground, a broad empty expanse of water in the middle, low hills in the distance. There are no people and no boats, only minimal ink and a poem. Ni Zan uses a dry side-tipped brush; lines are light and rough, like breath left on paper.

This extreme emptiness is not incompletion but choice: he reduces the world to trees, rock, water and a strip of sky. The turmoil of the late Yuan and one man's solitary purity are pressed into that void.
ni-zan-woods-valleys-1355.creator: Ni Zan

parmigianino-madonna-long-neck-1535.title: Madonna with the Long Neck
parmigianino-madonna-long-neck-1535.note:
Madonna with the Long Neck stages the Virgin, Child and a crowd of angels in an uncertain space. The Virgin sits at the centre, her neck stretched impossibly long, her right hand touching the Child while her body seems ready to slide out of the frame; the Child is oversized, his sleeping pose almost like an antique sculpture. A row of slender columns at the right lacks capitals, and the background reads as both stage set and unfinished architecture.

Parmigianino deliberately violates proportion and perspective, pushing grace to the edge of imbalance. This aesthetic, later called Mannerism, no longer trusts Renaissance measurement; it trusts line, pose and the viewer's unease.
parmigianino-madonna-long-neck-1535.creator: Parmigianino

pissarro-boulevard-montmartre-night-1897.title: The Boulevard Montmartre at Night
pissarro-boulevard-montmartre-night-1897.note:
The Boulevard Montmartre at Night is one of a series Pissarro painted looking down on the street from a Paris hotel window. The boulevard runs diagonally away to the right, streetlamps turning wet asphalt into lines of gold; carriages, pedestrians and shop windows are compressed into short strokes. The sky is deep blue, the buildings black silhouettes.

Pissarro was troubled by eye disease in his late years, yet found a new freedom in this urban series: he no longer painted the countryside but the rhythm and light of the modern city. The Impressionist "instant" becomes the night pulse of a metropolis.
pissarro-boulevard-montmartre-night-1897.creator: Camille Pissarro

raphael-school-of-athens-1511.title: The School of Athens
raphael-school-of-athens-1511.note:
In the Stanza della Segnatura, Raphael painted an ideal academy of antiquity. Plato and Aristotle stand beneath the central arch, one pointing to heaven, the other to earth; Socrates, Pythagoras, Euclid and Ptolemy are distributed to either side, arguing, calculating or listening. The architecture opens as a Bramante-like centralised space, its perspective drawing the crowd into a deep hall.

Raphael turned the humanists' image of ancient knowledge into an ordered conversation, and allowed his own contemporaries to enter the scene under different guises. The balance is not static: it is continually exchanged through gesture, gaze and the direction of bodies.
raphael-school-of-athens-1511.creator: Raphael

rembrandt-night-watch-1642.title: The Night Watch
rembrandt-night-watch-1642.note:
The Night Watch is not actually a night scene. A militia company marches out of an Amsterdam archway. Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, in black with a red sash, reaches towards the glove of his lieutenant, Willem van Ruytenburch, who wears yellow and points a lance beyond the frame. Some men drum, some raise a flag, some handle weapons; a small girl is picked out by light in the middle of the crowd.

Rembrandt refuses the conventional row-by-row group portrait and paints the company as a moment of assembly. Light and shadow move through the crowd; everyone is in motion and everyone is seen. The later title "Night Watch" came from darkened varnish; cleaning revealed a daytime departure.
rembrandt-night-watch-1642.creator: Rembrandt van Rijn

rembrandt-self-portrait-1669.title: Self-Portrait with Two Circles
rembrandt-self-portrait-1669.note:
Self-Portrait with Two Circles is the quietest of Rembrandt's late self-portraits. He sits at his easel with brush and palette, turning towards the viewer; on the wall behind, two circles are sketched in pale paint, like a geometry exercise or an unfinished manifesto. The face is lit, the corners of eye and mouth drawn down, the skin no longer young.

Rembrandt painted dozens of self-portraits; this one has no dramatic action, only a man in his studio facing old age calmly. What the two circles mean has never been settled; they leave the picture like an equation still to be solved.
rembrandt-self-portrait-1669.creator: Rembrandt van Rijn

renoir-bal-moulin-galette-1876.title: Bal du moulin de la Galette
renoir-bal-moulin-galette-1876.note:
Bal du moulin de la Galette shows a summer dance in the open air on the Montmartre hill. Crowds move between tree shadow and sunlight; at a table in the foreground people sit and talk, while dancers turn at the centre. Leaves cut the light into fragments that fall across clothes, hats and faces.

Renoir paints not isolated figures but the air between people: laughter, sweat, perfume, tobacco and shade mixed together. It is both the most joyful of Impressionist paintings and a visual record of nineteenth-century Parisian leisure.
renoir-bal-moulin-galette-1876.creator: Pierre-Auguste Renoir

repin-barge-haulers-1873.title: Barge Haulers on the Volga
repin-barge-haulers-1873.note:
Barge Haulers on the Volga shows a team of eleven men hauling a rope along the river, bodies leaning forward, feet sunk in sand. At the front an old man stares ahead; behind him a younger man tries to lift his head. The broad river, a distant boat and a hot sky lie behind them.

As a student Repin travelled the Volga and began the picture after seeing the haulers. He turns Russian poverty and endurance into a physical epic: no heroes, only people joined by a rope.
repin-barge-haulers-1873.creator: Ilya Repin

rubens-descent-from-cross-1614.title: The Descent from the Cross
rubens-descent-from-cross-1614.note:
Rubens's Descent from the Cross, the central panel of a triptych for Antwerp Cathedral, shows Christ's body sliding diagonally from the cross, caught in a white sheet. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus haul the cloth from above, John receives the feet below, and the Virgin, Mary Magdalene and other women kneel at the left. The figures form a rotating diamond, light running along the sheet and across muscle.

Rubens pushes Baroque weight, motion and blood to an extreme: this is not quiet mourning but a hauling that is still under way. The white cloth is both shroud and reflector, turning every gaze towards the body.
rubens-descent-from-cross-1614.creator: Peter Paul Rubens

sargent-madame-x-1884.title: Madame X (Madame Pierre Gautreau)
sargent-madame-x-1884.note:
Madame X portrays Virginie Amélie Avegno Gautreau, a celebrated Parisian beauty. She stands in profile, one hand resting on a table, her head thrown back to reveal a pale face and nose; the strap of her black satin dress has slipped, skin and fabric set in cold contrast.

The picture caused a scandal at the 1884 Salon: not for nudity but for a posture too proud, too ungovernable. Sargent later repainted the strap, yet the provocation did not disappear. It remains one of the sharpest portraits of the late-nineteenth-century "new woman."
sargent-madame-x-1884.creator: John Singer Sargent
sargent-madame-x-1884.holding: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

schiele-self-portrait-1912.title: Self-Portrait with Chinese Lantern Plant
schiele-self-portrait-1912.note:
Self-Portrait with Chinese Lantern Plant shows Schiele himself: thin body, shoulders raised, head tilted, eyes wide; his right hand twisted across his chest, fingers like twigs. At the right hangs a Chinese lantern plant, its orange calyces like small lamps. The background is blank, with almost no space.

Schiele makes the self-portrait a physiological and psychological exposure: the body uncomfortable, the expression alert, like an animal that has been seen. That taut line is the sharpest edge of Viennese Expressionism.
schiele-self-portrait-1912.creator: Egon Schiele

seurat-grande-jatte-1886.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
seurat-grande-jatte-1886.note:
A Sunday on La Grande Jatte shows a park beside the Seine: people sit on grass, hold parasols, walk dogs, row boats, all like silhouettes paused mid-motion. The surface is built from countless small dots of colour; from a distance they read as unified green and blue, up close as grains of orange, violet and yellow. Figures are reduced to vertical and horizontal blocks, even shadows measured as if by ruler.

Seurat brings colour science, optical theory and classical composition into one picture. It extends Impressionism's interest in light and contradicts its "instant": everything here is still and calculable, a specimen of modern city life.
seurat-grande-jatte-1886.creator: Georges Seurat

shen-zhou-loft-mount-lu-1467.title: Lofty Mount Lu
shen-zhou-loft-mount-lu-1467.note:
Lofty Mount Lu was painted by Shen Zhou for his teacher Chen Kuan's seventieth birthday. The mountain rises almost beyond the top of the picture, built with hemp-fibre texture strokes and ink graded from dark to pale; at its foot are a stream, pines and a figure gazing up at a waterfall. The inscription at the right states that the painting is for a teacher's birthday.

Shen Zhou makes Mount Lu a symbol of knowledge and virtue, not merely scenery. The literati taste of the Wu School appears here as a gentle but firm order: mountain high, water long, person small — but still looking.
shen-zhou-loft-mount-lu-1467.creator: Shen Zhou

shitao-thirty-six-peaks-1705.title: Thirty-six Peaks of Mount Huang Recollected
shitao-thirty-six-peaks-1705.note:
Thirty-six Peaks of Mount Huang Recollected is a late hanging scroll by Shitao, painted from memory. The composition stacks upward: pines and a thatched hut in the foreground, boulders, stream and cloud in the middle, peak heads receding almost to the top edge. Wet and dry brush alternate, ink running from dense black to pale grey as if washed by mist; a long inscription at the upper right records the occasion.

Shitao travelled through Huangshan many times and repainted it from memory in Yangzhou in old age. He does not reproduce a particular peak but compresses the mountain's strangeness into a stroke: mountains turn, clouds break, trees lean. In his Huayulu he proposed "one-stroke" — the world begins and is held together by a single brushstroke; this painting is that "one" made visible.
shitao-thirty-six-peaks-1705.creator: Shitao
shitao-thirty-six-peaks-1705.holding: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

today-01-01-arc2.title: With its Long Range Reconnaissance Imager (LORRI), New Horizons has observed several Kuiper Belt objects (KBOs) and dwarf planets at unique phase angles, as well as Centaurs at extremely high phase angles to search for forward-scattering rings or dust. These December 2017 false-color images of KBOs 2012 HZ84 (left) and 2012 HE85 are, for now, the farthest from Earth ever captured by a spacecraft. They're also the closest-ever images of Kuiper Belt objects.

today-01-01-img2.title:
An Atlas V 551 (AV-10) Rocket with the New Horizons Spacecraft is on launch pad 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Station. The Blue Sky and the Atlantic Ocean is seen in the Background.
Original caption: "KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, FLA. – With the backdrop of blue sky and blue water of the Atlantic Ocean, the Atlas V expendable launch vehicle with the New Horizons spacecraft (center) is nearly ready for launch. Surrounding the rocket are lightning masts that support the catenary wire used to provide lightning protection. The liftoff is scheduled for 1:24 p.m. EST Jan. 17. After its launch aboard the Atlas V, the compact, 1,050-pound piano-sized probe will get a boost from a kick-stage solid propellant motor for its journey to Pluto. New Horizons will be the fastest spacecraft ever launched, reaching lunar orbit distance in just nine hours and passing Jupiter 13 months later. The New Horizons science payload, developed under direction of Southwest Research Institute, includes imaging infrared and ultraviolet spectrometers, a multi-color camera, a long-range telescopic camera, two particle spectrometers, a space-dust detector and a radio science experiment. The dust counter was designed and built by students at the University of Colorado, Boulder. A launch before Feb. 3 allows New Horizons to fly past Jupiter in early 2007 and use the planet’s gravity as a slingshot toward Pluto. The Jupiter flyby trims the trip to Pluto by as many as five years and provides opportunities to test the spacecraft’s instruments and flyby capabilities on the Jupiter system. New Horizons could reach the Pluto system as early as mid-2015, conducting a five-month-long study possible only from the close-up vantage of a spacecraft."

today-01-01-img4.title: The fairing enclosing New Horizons awaits further processing upon its arrival atop a Lockheed Martin Atlas V launch vehicle in the Vertical Integration Facility at Complex 41 on Cape Canaveral Air Force Station. New Horizons carries seven scientific instruments that will characterize the global geology and geomorphology of Pluto and its moon Charon, map their surface compositions and temperatures, and examine Pluto's complex atmosphere. After that, flybys of Kuiper Belt objects from even farther in the solar system may be undertaken in an extended mission. New Horizons is the first mission in NASA's New Frontiers program of medium-class planetary missions. The spacecraft, designed for NASA by the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Md., will launch aboard a Lockheed Martin Atlas V rocket and fly by Pluto and Charon as early as summer 2015.

today-01-02-img1.title: This color picture is made from images taken by the imaging system on the Galileo spacecraft about 14 minutes before its closest approach to asteroid 243 Ida on August 28, 1993. The range from the spacecraft was about 10,500 kilometers (6,500 miles). The images used are from the sequence in which Ida's moon was originally discovered; the moon is visible to the right of the asteroid. This picture is made from images through the 4100-angstrom (violet), 7560 A (infrared) and 9680 A (infrared) filters. The color is 'enhanced' in the sense that the CCD camera is sensitive to near infrared wavelengths of light beyond human vision; a 'natural' color picture of this asteroid would appear mostly gray. Shadings in the image indicate changes in illumination angle on the many steep slopes of this irregular body as well as subtle color variations due to differences in the physical state and composition of the soil (regolith). There are brighter areas, appearing bluish in the picture, around craters on the upper left end of Ida, around the small bright crater near the center of the asteroid, and near the upper right-hand edge (the limb). This is a combination of more reflected blue light and greater absorption of near infrared light, suggesting a difference in the abundance or composition of iron-bearing minerals in these areas. Ida's moon also has a deeper near-infrared absorption and a different color in the violet than any area on this side of Ida. The moon is not identical in spectral properties to any area of Ida in view here, though its overall similarity in reflectance and general spectral type suggests that it is made of the same rock types basically. These data, combined with study of further imaging data and more detailed spectra from the Near Infrared Mapping Spectrometer, may allow scientists to determine whether the larger parent body of which Ida, its moon, and some other asteroids are fragments was a heated, differentiated object or made of relatively unaltered primitive chondritic material.

today-01-02-img2.title:
Pluto's image taken by New Horizons on July 14, 2015, from a range of 22,025 miles (35,445 kilometers). The striking features on Pluto are clearly visible, including the bright expanse of Pluto's icy, nitrogen-and-methane rich "heart," Sputnik Planitia.
The natural-looking colors result from refined calibration of data gathered by New Horizons' color Multispectral Visible Imaging Camera (MVIC). The processing creates images that would approximate the colors that the human eye would perceive, bringing them closer to “true color” than the images released at the time of the encounter. 

The source single-color MVIC scan includes no added data from other New Horizons imagers or instruments.

This aircraft crashed into the Red Sea after take off from Sharm el Sheikh, Egypt, on January 3, 2004 killing all 142 passengers, many of them French tourists, and all 6 crew members. Flight 604 - destination Paris Charles de Gaulle - has the highest death toll of any aviation accident in Egypt, and the highest death toll of any accident involving a Boeing 737-300.

In 2002 Swiss aviation authorities performed a surprise inspection on SU-ZCF, a Flash Airlines Boeing 737-300. They discovered missing pilot oxygen masks, a lack of oxygen tanks, and inoperable cockpit instruments. The Swiss grounded the aircraft until Flash repaired the plane. Several days later Switzerland banned Flash. In addition, Poland banned Flash. Tour operators in Norway ceased contracting with Flash. The crash of Flight 604 led to an investigation that exposed poor safety measures and helped lead to the folding of Flash.

today-01-04-img1.title: Mars Rover Curiosity in Artist's Concept, Tall - This artist concept features NASA's Mars Science Laboratory Curiosity rover, a mobile robot for investigating Mars' past or present ability to sustain microbial life. Curiosity launched in the fall of 2011 and landed successfully near Gale Crater in Aug of 2012. In this image, the mast, or rover's "head," rises to about 2.1 meters (6.9 feet) above ground level, about as tall as a basketball player. This mast supports two remote-sensing instruments: the Mast Camera, or "eyes," for stereo color viewing of surrounding terrain and material collected by the arm; and, the ChemCam instrument, which is a laser that vaporizes material from rocks up to about 9 meters (30 feet) away and determines what elements the rocks are made of.

today-01-04-img2.title: Amid billows of smoke and steam, the Delta II rocket with its Mars Exploration Rover (MER-A) payload lifts off the pad on time at 1:58 p.m. EDT from Launch Complex 17-A, Cape Canaveral Air Force Station. MER-A, known as Spirit, is the first of two rovers being launched to Mars. When the two rovers arrive at the red planet in 2004, they will bounce to airbag-cushioned landings at sites offering a balance of favorable conditions for safe landings and interesting science. The rovers see sharper images, can explore farther and examine rocks better than anything that has ever landed on Mars. The designated site for the MER-A mission is Gusev Crater, which appears to have been a crater lake. The second rover, MER-B, is scheduled to launch June 25.

today-01-04-img3.title: KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla. - In the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility, the Mars Exploration Rover-2 (MER-2) is tested for mobility and maneuverability. Set to launch in Spring 2003, the MER Mission will consist of two identical rovers designed to cover roughly 110 yards each Martian day. Each rover will carry five scientific instruments that will allow it to search for evidence of liquid water that may have been present in the planet's past. The rovers will be identical to each other, but will land at different regions of Mars. The first rover has a launch window opening May 30, and the second rover a window opening June 25. MER-B rover was inducted into the Robot Hall of Fame in 2010.

today-01-04-img4.title:
This artist's conception illustrates Kepler-22b, a planet known to comfortably circle in the habitable zone of a sun-like star. It is the first planet that NASA's Kepler mission has confirmed to orbit in a star's habitable zone -- the region around a star where liquid water, a requirement for life on Earth, could persist. The planet is 2.4 times the size of Earth, making it the smallest yet found to orbit in the middle of the habitable zone of a star like our sun.
Scientists do not yet know if the planet has a predominantly rocky, gaseous or liquid composition. It's possible that the world would have clouds in its atmosphere, as depicted here in the artist's interpretation.

today-01-05-arc2.title:
Approximate true-color image of Ceres, using the F7 ('red'), F2 ('green') and F8 ('blue') filters, projected onto a clear filter image. 
Images were acquired by Dawn at 04:13 UT May 4, 2015, at a distance of 13641 km. At the time, Dawn was over Ceres' northern hemisphere. The prominent, bright crater at right is Haulani. The smaller bright spot to its left is exposed on the floor of Oxo. Ejecta from these impacts appears to have exposed high albedo material similar to deposits found on the floor of Occator Crater. 

Image Credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech / UCLA / MPS / DLR / IDA / Justin Cowart

today-01-05-arc4.title:
This is a mosaic image, one of the largest ever taken by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, of the Crab Nebula, a six-light-year-wide expanding remnant of a star's supernova explosion. Japanese and Chinese astronomers recorded this violent event in 1054 CE.
The orange filaments are the tattered remains of the star and consist mostly of hydrogen. The rapidly spinning neutron star embedded in the center of the nebula is the dynamo powering the nebula's eerie interior bluish glow. The blue light comes from electrons whirling at nearly the speed of light around magnetic field lines from the neutron star. The neutron star, like a lighthouse, ejects twin beams of radiation that appear to pulse 30 times a second due to the neutron star's rotation. A neutron star is the crushed ultra-dense core of the exploded star.
The Crab Nebula derived its name from its appearance in a drawing made by Irish astronomer Lord Rosse in 1844, using a 36-inch telescope. When viewed by Hubble, as well as by large ground-based telescopes such as the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, the Crab Nebula takes on a more detailed appearance that yields clues into the spectacular demise of a star, 6,500 light-years away.

The newly composed image was assembled from 24 individual Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 exposures taken in October 1999, January 2000, and December 2000. The colors in the image indicate the different elements that were expelled during the explosion. Blue in the filaments in the outer part of the nebula represents neutral oxygen, green is singly-ionized sulfur, and red indicates doubly-ionized oxygen.

today-01-05-img1.note:
This is a mosaic image, one of the largest ever taken by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, of the Crab Nebula, a six-light-year-wide expanding remnant of a star's supernova explosion. Japanese and Chinese astronomers recorded this violent event in 1054 CE.
The orange filaments are the tattered remains of the star and consist mostly of hydrogen. The rapidly spinning neutron star embedded in the center of the nebula is the dynamo powering the nebula's eerie interior bluish glow. The blue light comes from electrons whirling at nearly the speed of light around magnetic field lines from the neutron star. The neutron star, like a lighthouse, ejects twin beams of radiation that appear to pulse 30 times a second due to the neutron star's rotation. A neutron star is the crushed ultra-dense core of the exploded star.
The Crab Nebula derived its name from its appearance in a drawing made by Irish astronomer Lord Rosse in 1844, using a 36-inch telescope. When viewed by Hubble, as well as by large ground-based telescopes such as the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, the Crab Nebula takes on a more detailed appearance that yields clues into the spectacular demise of a star, 6,500 light-years away.

The newly composed image was assembled from 24 individual Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 exposures taken in October 1999, January 2000, and December 2000. The colors in the image indicate the different elements that were expelled during the explosion. Blue in the filaments in the outer part of the nebula represents neutral oxygen, green is singly-ionized sulfur, and red indicates doubly-ionized oxygen.
